theme: Solomon’s wisdom; the golden age begins
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 3:1-5:18. Solomon asks for wisdom, shows it in the case of the two women, and builds a flourishing kingdom. Notice both the glory and the small warnings.
settingTheScene: Solomon’s reign begins with a political marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter and with worship at the high places, which are small signs that things are not perfect. At Gibeon, God appears to him in a dream and offers him whatever he asks. These chapters show the fulfillment of the promise to Abraham: a peaceful, prosperous Israel with influence over the nations. Solomon prepares to build the temple.
observation: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter, and “only, the people were sacrificing at the high places” (3:1-3).
God says, “Ask what I shall give you” (3:5).

Solomon answers, “I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in… Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (3:7-9).
“It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this” (3:10). God gives wisdom, riches, and honor (3:11-14).
Two women claim the same baby, and Solomon proposes to divide it. The true mother says, “Give her the living child” (3:16-28).
“Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy” (4:20).
“God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, like the sand on the seashore” (4:29).
Solomon writes 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs, and people come from all nations to hear his wisdom (4:32-34).
interpretation:
Solomon’s prayer at Gibeon is a model of humility. He calls himself a little child, aware of his inadequacy. He asks not for wealth, or long life, or the death of enemies, but for an understanding heart. God is pleased, and gives him what he asked and what he did not. The principle is stated elsewhere in the Bible: “Seek first the kingdom of God… and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

The story of the two women shows what the wisdom looks like in practice. It is not abstract. It is the ability to see through a deadlock and reveal the truth. “All Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him.” Wisdom from God allows a ruler to administer justice.

Chapter 4 describes the kingdom at its height. The people are as many as the sand by the sea, and “each man under his vine and under his fig tree.” It is the fulfillment of the promise to Abraham and a taste of the peace that God wants for his people. The description of Solomon’s wisdom is stunning: greater than that of all the people of the East. Nations send ambassadors.

But there are quiet warnings, if you read carefully. The marriage alliance with Egypt, the lingering practice of high places, and the long lists of provisions all hint at a king who is gathering what Deuteronomy 17 told kings not to gather: wives, horses, and wealth. The text does not tell us this yet, but it plants the question.

The treaty with Hiram of Tyre in chapter 5 prepares for the temple. It also shows the cost: forced labor. “King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel.” The shadow of oppression begins.
connection: Jesus is “greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42). He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30), and in him are “hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). James 1:5 says, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach.” The peace of Solomon’s reign points to the peace that Christ brings (Ephesians 2:14).
application:
Pray Solomon’s prayer today. Ask for an understanding mind to do what God has given you to do.

Notice what you ask God for most often. What does that reveal?

Look for the quiet warnings in your own life, small compromises that seem harmless now.
prayerPrompts: Ask God for an understanding mind and a discerning heart.
Thank him for Jesus, the wisdom of God, greater than Solomon.
Ask him to keep you from small compromises.
